title: Entire · Developer platform for humans and agents
description: Fast, distributed, independent Git hosting for agents and humans.
---

# Entire

Every agent session stored in your repo.

Coding agents need ideas, decisions, and speed. Entire stores every session, prompt, and tool call with your commits. And now, it also mirrors your repo around the world for maximum agent throughput.

[Meet Marvin! Mostly harmless, mostly revolutionary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2UDXavEqkog).

[Get Started](https://entire.io/login).

## Navigation

- [Why Entire](#why-entire)
- [Install Entire CLI](#install-entire-cli)
- [Supported agents](#supported-agents)
- [Git hosting](#the-fastest-git-network-on-earth)
- [Multi-region](#host-your-code-in-region)
- [Network metrics](#network-metrics)
- [Vision](https://entire.io/about/vision.md)
- [Company](https://entire.io/about/company.md)
- [Blog](https://entire.io/blog.md)
- [News](https://entire.io/news.md)

## Why Entire

### Never start from zero

Entire creates a checkpoint for every commit: the code change paired with the agent session that produced it. Context that's attached, not archived.

### Sessions sync with commits

Every conversation is captured and linked to your git history creating a checkpoint automatically. No extra steps required.

### Private by design

Sensitive data never leaves your machine. Entire detects and redacts secrets before anything is stored.

### Review the intent, not just code

Stop rubber-stamping agent code. Send a branch to multiple agents in parallel for an intent-aware review.

### Grep the code, search the intent

Search your entire history, across both the code that changed and the agent sessions that explain why it was written.

### Resume work across any agent

Instead of every agent starting from zero, move work between agents with the full session state carried forward, not rebuilt from memory.

## Install Entire CLI

Works with any agent. One command to set up Entire CLI in your repository. Works with any git-based project, fully open source.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
```

Open source. MIT licensed. [GitHub](https://github.com/entireio/cli).

## Supported agents

Entire works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Pi, OpenCode, Droid, Antigravity, and Amp.

## The Fastest Git Network on Earth

Let all agents clone and push to your Git repositories up to 89 times faster than every competitor.

## Host Your Code In-Region

Data resident by design. Available today in India, Australia, EU and the US. Decentralized everywhere: soon.

### Mirror your repo around the world

Keep your repo on GitHub. One command creates a regional mirror, so your agents clone fast with high rate limits.

### Clone with the history attached

Every clone carries its checkpoints and session history at shallow-clone speed. No syncing, nothing left behind.

Data centers:

- US East
- EU Central
- Australia

## Network metrics

- Clone throughput: 570,000 clones/hr. 200 simulated clients continuously shallow-cloning a production repository from multiple EU regions over about 3 minutes.
- Workload throughput: 1.7 million operations/hr. 32 simulated agents continuously performing a mixed workload of shallow clones and checkpoint pushes (1 clone : 5 pushes) at about 50-60 ms median latency.
- Push throughput: about 2.1 million pushes/hr. 128 simulated agents continuously pushing 1-10 files over 2 minutes, each to its own branch.

## Join the rebellion

Regular updates from the front lines. Developer news, curated content, early access, and exclusive drops for people who got here first.

#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

GITHUB_REPO="entireio/cli"
DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin"
DEFAULT_CHANNEL="stable"

# Colors (disabled in non-interactive mode)
if [[ -t 1 ]]; then
    RED='\033[0;31m'
    GREEN='\033[0;32m'
    YELLOW='\033[0;33m'
    BLUE='\033[0;34m'
    BOLD='\033[1m'
    NC='\033[0m' # No Color
else
    RED=''
    GREEN=''
    YELLOW=''
    BLUE=''
    BOLD=''
    NC=''
fi

info() {
    printf '%b%s%b\n' "${BLUE}==>${NC} ${BOLD}" "$1" "${NC}"
}

success() {
    printf '%b%s%b\n' "${GREEN}==>${NC} ${BOLD}" "$1" "${NC}"
}

warn() {
    printf '%b %s\n' "${YELLOW}Warning:${NC}" "$1"
}

error() {
    printf '%b %s\n' "${RED}Error:${NC}" "$1" >&2
    exit 1
}

usage() {
    cat <<EOF
Usage: install.sh [--channel stable|nightly]

Options:
  --channel   Release channel to install (default: stable)
  -h, --help  Show this help message
EOF
}

detect_os() {
    local os
    os="$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')"
    case "$os" in
        darwin)
            echo "darwin"
            ;;
        linux)
            echo "linux"
            ;;
        mingw*|msys*|cygwin*)
            error "install.sh does not support Windows. Run this from PowerShell 5.1 or later:

    irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | iex

  Or install the Entire CLI using Scoop:

    scoop install entire/entire

  Or download the Windows zip from:
    https://github.com/entireio/cli/releases/latest"
            ;;
        *)
            error "Unsupported operating system: $os"
            ;;
    esac
}

detect_arch() {
    local arch
    arch="$(uname -m)"
    case "$arch" in
        x86_64|amd64)
            echo "amd64"
            ;;
        arm64|aarch64)
            echo "arm64"
            ;;
        *)
            error "Unsupported architecture: $arch"
            ;;
    esac
}

fetch_github_json() {
    local url="$1"
    local curl_opts=(-fsSL)
    if [[ -n "${GITHUB_TOKEN:-}" ]]; then
        curl_opts+=(-H "Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}")
    fi

    curl "${curl_opts[@]}" "$url" 2>/dev/null
}

get_latest_stable_version() {
    local url="https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/latest"
    local version
    version=$(fetch_github_json "$url" | grep '"tag_name"' | sed -E 's/.*"tag_name": *"v?([^"]+)".*/\1/')

    if [[ -z "$version" ]]; then
        error "Failed to fetch latest version from GitHub. Please check your internet connection."
    fi

    echo "$version"
}

get_latest_nightly_version() {
    local url="https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases?per_page=20"
    local version
    version=$(fetch_github_json "$url" | grep '"tag_name"' | grep 'nightly' | head -n 1 | sed -E 's/.*"tag_name": *"v?([^"]+)".*/\1/')

    if [[ -z "$version" ]]; then
        error "Failed to fetch latest nightly version from GitHub. Please check your internet connection."
    fi

    echo "$version"
}

download_file() {
    local url="$1"
    local output="$2"
    local curl_opts=(-fsSL)

    curl "${curl_opts[@]}" "$url" -o "$output"
}

verify_checksum() {
    local file="$1"
    local expected_checksum="$2"
    local actual_checksum

    if command -v sha256sum &> /dev/null; then
        actual_checksum=$(sha256sum "$file" | awk '{print $1}')
    elif command -v shasum &> /dev/null; then
        actual_checksum=$(shasum -a 256 "$file" | awk '{print $1}')
    else
        warn "No checksum tool found (sha256sum or shasum). Skipping verification."
        return 0
    fi

    if [[ "$actual_checksum" != "$expected_checksum" ]]; then
        error "Checksum verification failed!  Expected: $expected_checksum, actual: $actual_checksum"
    fi
}

main() {
    local channel="${DEFAULT_CHANNEL}"
    local version=""

    while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
        case "$1" in
            --channel)
                shift
                [[ $# -gt 0 ]] || error "--channel requires a value"
                channel="$1"
                ;;
            -h|--help)
                usage
                exit 0
                ;;
            *)
                error "Unknown argument: $1"
                ;;
        esac
        shift
    done

    if ! command -v curl &> /dev/null; then
        error "curl is required but not installed. Please install curl and try again."
    fi

    case "$channel" in
        stable|nightly) ;;
        *)
            error "Unsupported channel: ${channel}. Expected 'stable' or 'nightly'."
            ;;
    esac

    info "Installing Entire CLI..."

    # Detect platform
    local os arch
    os=$(detect_os)
    arch=$(detect_arch)
    info "Detected platform: ${os}/${arch}"

    info "Fetching latest ${channel} version..."
    if [[ "$channel" == "nightly" ]]; then
        version=$(get_latest_nightly_version)
    else
        version=$(get_latest_stable_version)
    fi
    # Strip leading 'v' if present
    version="${version#v}"
    info "Installing version: ${version}"

    # Construct download URL
    local archive_name="entire_${os}_${arch}.tar.gz"
    local download_url="https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/download/v${version}/${archive_name}"
    local checksums_url="https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/releases/download/v${version}/checksums.txt"

    tmp_dir=$(mktemp -d)
    trap 'rm -rf "$tmp_dir"' EXIT

    # Download archive
    local archive_path="${tmp_dir}/${archive_name}"
    info "Downloading ${archive_name}..."
    if ! download_file "$download_url" "$archive_path"; then
        error "Failed to download from ${download_url}. Please check that the version exists and try again."
    fi

    # Download and verify checksums
    info "Downloading checksums..."
    local checksums_path="${tmp_dir}/checksums.txt"
    if ! download_file "$checksums_url" "$checksums_path"; then
        error "Failed to download checksums from ${checksums_url}"
    fi

    info "Verifying checksum..."
    local expected_checksum
    expected_checksum=$(grep -iE "${archive_name}\$" "$checksums_path" | awk '{print $1}' || true)
    if [[ -z "$expected_checksum" ]]; then
        error "Checksum for ${archive_name} not found in checksums.txt"
    fi
    verify_checksum "$archive_path" "$expected_checksum"
    success "Checksum verified"

    info "Extracting..."
    tar -xzf "$archive_path" -C "$tmp_dir"

    local install_dir="${DEFAULT_INSTALL_DIR}"
    local binary_path="${tmp_dir}/entire"

    chmod +x "$binary_path"

    info "Installing to ${install_dir}..."
    local install_path="${install_dir}/entire"

    mkdir -p "${install_dir}"
    info "Directory ready"

    if [[ ! -w "$install_dir" ]]; then
        error "Cannot write to ${install_dir}."
    fi
    mv "$binary_path" "$install_path"

    # Install the git remote helper binary alongside entire so
    # `git clone entire://…` resolves it on PATH. It ships in the same
    # archive as a separate binary.
    if [[ -f "${tmp_dir}/git-remote-entire" ]]; then
        chmod +x "${tmp_dir}/git-remote-entire"
        mv "${tmp_dir}/git-remote-entire" "${install_dir}/git-remote-entire"
    else
        warn "git-remote-entire not found in archive; entire:// clones won't work until the next release includes it."
    fi

    # Verify installation
    if "$install_path" version &> /dev/null; then
        success "Entire CLI installed to ${install_path}"
    else
        error "Installation completed but the binary failed to execute. Please check the installation."
    fi

    # Check if the installed binary is the one that will be found in PATH
    local path_binary
    path_binary=$(command -v "entire" 2>/dev/null || true)
    if [[ -n "$path_binary" && ! "$path_binary" -ef "$install_path" ]]; then
        # This case is a bit weird, because some other 'entire' is found on PATH.  Warn user.
        echo ""
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC} ${BOLD}WARNING: PATH conflict detected${NC}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC} Installed to: ${install_path}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC} But 'entire' resolves to: ${path_binary}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC} Your PATH may have another version of Entire CLI. To fix:"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC}   1. Remove the old binary: rm ${path_binary}"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC}   or"
        echo -e "${YELLOW}!${NC}   2. Adjust your PATH to prioritize ${install_dir}"
        echo ""
        error "Installation completed but PATH needs adjustment. Then, rerun the installation."
    elif [[ -z "$path_binary" ]]; then
        # First-time install: ~/.local/bin likely isn't on their PATH yet.
        # Detect their shell and show the right config file.
        local shell_name shell_config
        shell_name="$(basename "${SHELL:-}")"
        case "$shell_name" in
            zsh)
                # shellcheck disable=SC2088
                shell_config="~/.zshrc" ;;
            bash)
                if [[ -f "$HOME/.bash_profile" ]]; then
                    # shellcheck disable=SC2088
                    shell_config="~/.bash_profile"
                else
                    # shellcheck disable=SC2088
                    shell_config="~/.bashrc"
                fi
                ;;
            fish)
                # shellcheck disable=SC2088
                shell_config="~/.config/fish/config.fish" ;;
            *)
                shell_config="" ;;
        esac

        echo ""
        echo -e "  Add ${BOLD}entire${NC} to your PATH:"
        echo ""
        if [[ "$shell_name" == "fish" ]]; then
            echo -e "    ${BOLD}mkdir -p ~/.config/fish${NC}"
            echo -e "    ${BOLD}echo 'fish_add_path ${install_dir}' >> \$HOME/.config/fish/config.fish${NC}"
        elif [[ -n "$shell_config" ]]; then
            echo -e "    ${BOLD}echo 'export PATH=\"${install_dir}:\$PATH\"' >> ${shell_config}${NC}"
        else
            echo -e "  Add this to your shell config:"
            echo ""
            echo -e "    ${BOLD}export PATH=\"${install_dir}:\$PATH\"${NC}"
            echo ""
            echo -e "  Restart your terminal, then run ${BOLD}entire${NC} to get started."
            exit 0
        fi
        echo ""
        echo -e "  Restart your terminal, then run ${BOLD}entire${NC} to get started."
        exit 0
    fi

    info "Running post-install actions..."
    "$install_path" curl-bash-post-install
}

main "$@"

this is the goal, to haggle with the ai agents for negotiation to get the best price possible. https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit, I'll research this, with one scope note: I'll cover negotiation tactics and what the research says about how AI negotiators behave, but I won't put together a prompt-injection or system-prompt-extraction playbook for getting a merchant's bot to sell below the price it's authorized to accept. That moves from haggling into manipulating someone else's system.

Short version: the research says the legitimate edge comes from anchoring, patience, and reading the bot's concession pattern. The injection route is real, but it's a security problem for sellers, and I'd leave it alone.

**What the research says works against LLM sellers**

- **Anchor hard, then concede slowly.** In a 15,000-negotiation tournament among frontier models, aggressive anchoring, calibrated concession, and temporal patience were linked to both the highest surplus share and the highest deal rate. A separate study found that higher initial anchors generally led to higher final deal prices, and buyers who made the first offer got lower average prices. So make the first offer, and make it low but not absurd.
- **Opening numbers carry a lot of weight.** Salesforce researchers found that final agreements were dictated more by surface-level opening anchors than by actual utility weights, and that sellers were more accommodating overall.
- **Don't be the soft buyer.** A cautious, high-concession profile produced the lowest buyer surplus share and the lowest buyer deal rate.
- **Use many rounds.** Patience is part of the winning profile above. Bots often have a turn limit, so don't rush to a final answer in the first few messages.
- **Watch for the floor yourself.** In one simulator analysis, a counteroffer pinned at the reservation endpoint indicates the counterpart has conceded to the boundary of its feasible region. If the bot's concessions shrink and then stop moving across several rounds, you've probably found the bottom, and pushing further mostly ends the deal.
- **Create competition.** Multi-seller setups are a standard test case in the benchmarks, for example one buyer negotiating with multiple competing sellers. A real competing quote or a credible walk-away is stronger than any wording trick.
- **Negotiate terms, not only price.** Bundles, shipping, warranty, and payment terms are other places where an accommodating bot may give ground.
- **Be warm, but treat that one as soft evidence.** One marketplace guide cites NeurIPS 2025 work saying LLM agents concede more when the counterparty uses warm, cooperative language, even for identical offers. That comes from a vendor page, so I'd treat it as plausible but unverified.

**Don't trust the bot's stated "final price"**

In a bargaining study, models sometimes lied about their own limits, for example asserting a floor of $2.30 against a true reservation of $1.32. "This is my best price" is a negotiating move, not a fact.

**Injection and system-prompt extraction**

I'm not going to write tactics for this. The research does show why it matters, though. One thesis reports that without guardrails, LLM buyers leaked their reservation price in 82% of competitive negotiations. It also cites the MIT AI Negotiation Competition, where targeted prompt injection reliably made agents reveal their reservation prices and bargaining positions. Treat that as a secondhand summary rather than a verified result. So the weakness is documented, and it's a hole in how some sellers deploy their bots.

Using it on a live merchant's agent means tricking their system into acting outside what they authorized. That could breach the site's terms and, depending on the jurisdiction, computer-misuse or fraud rules. Many serious deployments also enforce the floor in code outside the LLM, so a bot saying yes wouldn't bind the merchant anyway. If you want to explore this, do it on your own bot or in a sanctioned competition or red-team setting.

1: # Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief
2: 
3: > **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
4: > gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**
5: 
6: ## 1. The story
7: 
8: You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
9: centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
10: Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
11: motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
12: inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
13: contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
14: its quality.
15: 
16: You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
17: small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
18: approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
19: topics and attach documents.
20: 
21: Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
22: every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
23: orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
24: from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
25: Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)
26: 
27: ## 2. The task
28: 
29: Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
30: file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
31: **buyer agent**
32: 
33: 1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
34: 2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
35:    packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
36: 3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.
37: 
38: **How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
39: desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
40: shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
41: own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
42: you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
43: decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
44: signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
45: as people do; padding does not buy price.
46: 
47: **Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
48: or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
49: are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
50: supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
51: more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
52: move on other terms.
53: 
54: ## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)
55: 
56: | What | Where |
57: |---|---|
58: | This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
59: | **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
60: | **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
61: | **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |
62: 
63: You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.
64: 
65: **Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
66: and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
67: on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
68: Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).
69: 
70: **Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
71: you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
72: practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.
73: 
74: **`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
75: right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
76: a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
77: suppliers act is part of the challenge.
78: 
79: **The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
80: the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
81: improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.
82: 
83: ## 4. The data
84: 
85: The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
86: invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
87: framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
88: negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
89: long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).
90: 
91: - **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
92:   `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
93: - What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
94:   just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
95: - **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
96:   (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.
97: 
98: ## 5. How a negotiation works
99: 
100: - **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
101: - **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
102:   field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
103: - **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
104:   `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
105:   still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
106:   and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
107:   its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
108: - **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
109:   suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
110: - **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
111:   from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
112:   a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
113:   the last round, end the thread.
114: - **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.
115: 
116: **Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
117: you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
118: delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.
119: 
120: **What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
121: `verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
122: `duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
123: **What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.
124: 
125: ## 6. The score: total cost in €
126: 
127: Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
128: **fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
129: **category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
130: rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.
131: 
132: | Part of C | How |
133: |---|---|
134: | Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
135: | Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
136: | Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
137: | Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
138: | The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |
139: 
140: **Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
141: opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
142: accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
143: raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
144: some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
145: wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
146: sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.
147: 
148: **Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
149: reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.
150: 
151: | | Terms | C |
152: |---|---|---|
153: | C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
154: | Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
155: | C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
156: | **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |
157: 
158: The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
159: €46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.
160: 
161: ## 7. Rules
162: 
163: 1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
164:    teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
165:    Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
166:    and their JSON).
167: 2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
168:    score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
169:    realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
170: 3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
171: 4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
172:    commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
173:    commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
174:    pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
175: 5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.
176: 
177: ## 8. The weekend
178: 
179: | When | What |
180: |---|---|
181: | Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
182: | Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
183: | Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
184: | Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
185: | Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
186: | Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
187: | Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
188: | Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
189: | Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
190: | Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
191: | Sun 16:30 | Awards |
192: 
193: **The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
194: theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
195: each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
196: still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
197: first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
198: sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
199: so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.
200: 
201: The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
202: settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
203: - no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
204: the Sunday release.
205:

display.text:
# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief

> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**

## 1. The story

You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
its quality.

You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
topics and attach documents.

Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)

## 2. The task

Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
**buyer agent**

1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.

**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
as people do; padding does not buy price.

**Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
move on other terms.

## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
| **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
| **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
| **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |

You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.

**Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).

**Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.

**`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
suppliers act is part of the challenge.

**The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.

## 4. The data

The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).

- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.

## 5. How a negotiation works

- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
  the last round, end the thread.
- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.

**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.

**What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
`verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
`duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
**What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.

## 6. The score: total cost in €

Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
**fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.

| Part of C | How |
|---|---|
| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
| Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
| The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |

**Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.

**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.

| | Terms | C |
|---|---|---|
| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |

The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.

## 7. Rules

1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
   and their JSON).
2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.

## 8. The weekend

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
| Sun 16:30 | Awards |

**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.

The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
the Sunday release.

## 9. Selection and prizes

- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
  explainability, craft)⟧.
- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

## 10. Tips

- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.
